paragraphs: This paper addresses debiasing after a machine learning model has already been trained. It proposes a scalable post-processing algorithm that applies to both classical models and deep neural networks. Working at this stage makes the approach relevant when a trained model is already available, particularly for the large-scale models emphasized in the abstract.

The theoretical contribution is a near-optimality guarantee expressed through a bound on excess Bayes risk. This gives the method a formal assessment of how far its predictive risk can be from the relevant optimum. The claim is therefore more specific than simply saying that the algorithm reduces bias: it also controls the predictive cost associated with its solution.

Experiments on standard benchmark datasets cover classical learning algorithms and modern neural architectures. The authors report better results than earlier post-processing methods and performance comparable to methods that address debiasing during training. They also find the approach particularly effective for models trained at scale. Together, these findings support post-processing as a practical route to debiasing with both theoretical and empirical backing.
neurips-2021-a-near-optimal-algorithm-fo.tldr: A scalable post-processing method debiases trained models with a near-optimal risk guarantee and strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Generalization analysis asks how a learning algorithm’s performance on its training data relates to its performance beyond those data. Many analyses provide upper bounds, which can leave substantial uncertainty about the actual gap. This paper obtains an exact characterization of the expected generalization error for the Gibbs learning algorithm, also known as the Gibbs posterior.

The characterization uses symmetrized KL information between the training samples and the hypothesis produced by the algorithm. This quantity describes their statistical dependence through a symmetric combination of KL information. The result identifies that dependence as an exact ingredient in expected generalization error for this algorithm, giving it a stronger role than merely appearing in a potentially loose bound.

The authors show that their result can tighten existing expected-error and PAC-Bayesian bounds. They also extend the analysis to Gibbs learning with a data-dependent regularizer and to an asymptotic regime in which the algorithm approaches empirical risk minimization. These extensions make the characterization useful across several versions of Gibbs learning while retaining its focus on expected generalization.
neurips-2021-an-exact-characterization-o.tldr: The paper exactly characterizes the Gibbs algorithm’s expected generalization error using symmetrized KL information.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex optimization when an algorithm can request function values, but some responses may be arbitrarily corrupted. The corruption is attached to points in the domain: an adversary can alter their function values without restriction, provided the total volume of affected points stays bounded. The objective is to locate a point close to the true minimizer despite these misleading observations.

The first result establishes a fundamental limit on how accurately the minimizer can be located. Surprisingly, the obstruction persists even if the algorithm is allowed an unlimited number of queries. Under this corruption model, asking for more function evaluations cannot by itself remove the uncertainty introduced by the adversary.

The authors then develop an efficient algorithm whose distance from the minimizer matches the lower bound up to constant factors. This pairs an impossibility result with an achievable guarantee: the algorithm reaches essentially the accuracy permitted by the information available. The contribution is thus both a method for optimization under outliers and a characterization of the best attainable localization accuracy.
neurips-2021-approximate-optimization-of.tldr: An efficient convex optimization algorithm matches the accuracy limit imposed by arbitrarily corrupted function values.

paragraphs: Optimizing sequences, trees, or graphs becomes difficult when evaluating each candidate is expensive. Bayesian optimization tackles this by learning a surrogate for the unknown objective and using it to choose useful candidates. One approach maps discrete structures into a continuous latent space, searches there, and decodes selected points back into structures for evaluation.

The paper identifies a weakness in relying exclusively on that latent space. A deep generative model learns a representation of structures, but its representation may not emphasize the features needed to predict the particular objective being optimized. Consequently, the surrogate can miss useful structural information even when the generative model supplies a workable search space.

The proposed method, LADDER, introduces a structure-coupled kernel that combines the latent representation with information from decoded structures. This gives the surrogate access to both views of each candidate. On real-world benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements over optimization using only the latent space and results better than or similar to state-of-the-art methods. The findings support explicitly connecting structural information to surrogate prediction.
neurips-2021-combining-latent-space-and-.tldr: LADDER improves Bayesian optimization over discrete structures by combining latent representations with explicit structural information.

paragraphs: This paper estimates a distribution’s mean while protecting individual data through differential privacy. Its central challenge is handling unknown covariance, which describes how variation differs across directions. Accuracy is measured using Mahalanobis distance, so the error is judged relative to that covariance rather than on a single uniform scale.

The authors introduce two estimators. The first privately samples a point with approximately maximal Tukey depth, restricting the exponential mechanism to points with large depth. The second adds noise to the empirical mean using the empirical covariance to calibrate that noise. In the second method, covariance is used internally; only the estimated mean is released. Both approaches require careful preprocessing to establish privacy.

Informally, their sample requirement scales as dimension divided by squared target error. Earlier estimators with the same accuracy guarantee needed strong prior covariance bounds or at least dimension to the three-halves samples. The second estimator also has guarantees for subgaussian distributions, with somewhat worse dependence on the privacy parameter. The results show how covariance can inform private estimation without separately releasing a private covariance estimate.
neurips-2021-covariance-aware-private-me.tldr: Two private mean estimators adapt to unknown covariance while achieving strong sample-efficiency guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies distributed saddle-point optimization, where an objective is minimized in some variables and maximized in others. It considers convex-concave problems, including strongly convex-concave cases, across both centralized master-worker systems and decentralized mesh networks. A central assumption is that the local functions held by different nodes are similar, possibly because their data are statistically similar.

The authors establish lower bounds on the communication needed by a fairly general class of algorithms. In the strongly convex setting described, these bounds depend on the function-similarity parameter relative to strong convexity and logarithmically on the desired accuracy. Network structure also matters: the master-worker bound involves network diameter, while the mesh bound involves the communication matrix’s normalized eigengap.

They then propose algorithms that match the respective lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. This connects achievable performance to a theoretical communication limit for each network type. An evaluation on robust regression assesses the proposed methods in an application. The main implication is that local-function similarity and network connectivity can be incorporated explicitly into near-optimal communication guarantees.
neurips-2021-distributed-saddle-point-pr.tldr: Distributed saddle-point algorithms exploit similar local functions to match communication lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Fair classification often relies on protected attributes recorded in training data, but these attributes may be incorrect. This paper studies an adversarial version of that problem: an omniscient adversary may select a specified fraction of training samples and change their protected attributes arbitrarily. This captures errors that need not follow stochastic or independence assumptions.

The authors develop an optimization framework with provable accuracy and fairness guarantees under this corruption model. It supports multiple protected attributes, attributes with more than two possible values, and a broad family of fairness criteria called linear-fractional metrics. The framework can also accommodate perturbations beyond protected attributes, extending its scope beyond the primary motivating setting.

For natural hypothesis classes, the paper proves that its guarantees are nearly tight. No algorithm can substantially improve accuracy, and improving fairness beyond the guarantee requires sacrificing accuracy. This makes the result an account of the achievable tradeoff as well as a learning method. Experiments evaluate statistical rate on real and synthetic datasets against a family of adversaries.
neurips-2021-fair-classification-with-ad.tldr: A classification framework provides nearly tight accuracy and fairness guarantees when an adversary corrupts protected attributes.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving three or more objects, making them useful for datasets whose interactions cannot be captured fully by ordinary pairwise connections. This paper studies how to find bipartite components within such structures. Its goal is approximate discovery, allowing an algorithm to identify this organization without requiring an exact solution to the component-finding problem.

The central construction is a new heat diffusion process on a hypergraph. The authors use that process to design a polynomial-time algorithm for approximately finding bipartite components. Diffusion is therefore the basis of the computational method, connecting a process on the hypergraph to the task of identifying its internal structure.

The paper provides a theoretical performance guarantee and compares the algorithm with the previous state of the art on synthetic and real-world datasets. Across the tested range of hypergraphs, the authors report consistent and significant improvements. The combination of a proved guarantee and broad experimental comparison supports the new diffusion process as a useful tool for this particular structural analysis task.
neurips-2021-finding-bipartite-component.tldr: A new hypergraph heat diffusion process yields a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with theoretical guarantees and strong experimental results.

paragraphs: Learning object representations without supervision can support both image segmentation and scene generation organized around individual objects. Existing approaches face difficulties with visually complex images and with how they construct object representations. Recurrent models impose a sequence and scale poorly to large images, while iterative refinement requires initializing a fixed number of representations.

GENESIS-v2 instead learns pixel embeddings and groups them through differentiable clustering based on a stochastic stick-breaking process. This procedure produces randomly ordered object representations without initializing a fixed number of clusters in advance. The resulting model can infer a variable number of objects without recurrent networks or iterative refinement, directly addressing the representation choices highlighted by the authors.

The paper evaluates the model on established synthetic datasets and more complex real-world datasets. It reports strong performance relative to recent baselines for unsupervised segmentation and object-centric scene generation. These findings support embedding-based clustering as a practical route to flexible object representations, with evidence extending beyond the simpler visual settings that motivated the work.
neurips-2021-genesis-v2-inferring-unorde.tldr: GENESIS-v2 uses differentiable pixel clustering to infer a variable number of unordered object representations without recurrent networks or iterative refinement.

paragraphs: Adapting a model directly between very different source and target domains can be difficult. Gradual domain adaptation uses additional unlabeled data to provide intermediate steps between them. Its practical complication is that these data may arrive without labels identifying the intermediate domains or the order in which adaptation should proceed.

The proposed Intermediate DOmain Labeler, or IDOL, discovers that ordering through a coarse-to-fine process. It first trains domain discriminators progressively to obtain a rough sequence. It then refines the indexing using a cycle-consistency loss that encourages each next domain to preserve enough of the current domain’s discriminative knowledge. A gradual adaptation algorithm can subsequently use the discovered sequence.

On gradual adaptation benchmarks, the authors report performance comparable to or sometimes better than using predefined domain sequences. This suggests that manually supplied ordering is not always needed to obtain an effective adaptation path. The contribution makes gradual adaptation applicable to less organized unlabeled data and provides an empirical way to improve robustness to the quality of the domain sequence.
neurips-2021-gradual-domain-adaptation-w.tldr: IDOL discovers ordered intermediate domains from unlabeled data, enabling gradual adaptation without a predefined domain sequence.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can generate molecules by rewarding desirable properties, including docking scores that estimate protein binding. The paper identifies two obstacles: generated molecules may be chemically unacceptable, and docking-score optimization presents a difficult search landscape with many local optima. A useful generator therefore needs both chemical constraints and an effective exploration strategy.

FREED combines fragment-based molecule generation with error-prioritized experience replay. The fragment construction constrains candidates to a realistic, qualified chemical space, while the replay mechanism supports exploration within that space. The authors study both generation from scratch and scaffold-based generation, showing that the framework works in both schemes.

The reported molecules have higher quality than those from existing methods, and their docking scores reach state-of-the-art performance on two of three targets. Ablation studies also show significant performance improvements from the predictive-error replay variant, FREED(PE). These results concern generated-molecule quality and a simulated binding proxy; the stated contribution is a more effective way to search for promising molecular candidates using that feedback.
neurips-2021-hit-and-lead-discovery-with.tldr: FREED combines molecular fragments and error-prioritized replay to generate higher-quality molecules with strong docking scores.

paragraphs: Data augmentation changes the examples used during training, but its optimization effects depend on how those changes interact with the learning rate. This paper studies that interaction in linear regression with mean squared error. The convex setting allows a precise analysis while still revealing complicated behavior when augmentation and optimization schedules evolve together.

The authors interpret augmented gradient methods as stochastic optimization over a changing sequence of proxy losses. This creates a common framework for examining learning rate, batch size, and different augmentation mechanisms. The analysis covers arbitrary augmentation schemes, with additive noise and random projections illustrating the range of transformations considered.

The paper identifies joint learning-rate and augmentation schedules that guarantee convergence, characterizes the resulting minimum, and provides convergence rates. These are conditional guarantees about compatible schedules, rather than a claim that every augmentation schedule converges. Viewed through the proxy-loss framework, the results provide stochastic-approximation-style conditions for augmented gradient descent. Their significance is that augmentation affects the optimization process itself, including where it converges, even in this simple convex learning problem.
neurips-2021-how-data-augmentation-affec.tldr: A proxy-loss analysis explains how augmentation and learning-rate schedules jointly determine convergence in linear regression.

paragraphs: Agents trained together through self-play can develop arbitrary conventions that their teammates understand but unfamiliar partners do not. Zero-shot coordination asks whether independently trained agents can cooperate without first learning such shared conventions together. This paper studies that challenge in Hanabi, where coordination also matters when an agent joins an unfamiliar team.

An earlier method, Other-Play, uses known environment symmetries to discourage incompatible conventions. Obtaining those symmetries can itself be computationally difficult. The authors investigate a different route based on k-level reasoning, adapting it so that all reasoning levels are trained synchronously. This changes the training organization used to prepare agents for coordination.

The resulting method achieves competitive zero-shot coordination and ad-hoc teamplay performance in Hanabi, including partnerships with a human-like proxy bot. The authors also introduce SyKLRBR, which co-trains a best response and improves further on their synchronous k-level method. The evidence supports this training approach for the tested coordination setting, with the proxy-bot result specifically addressing a human-like partner rather than establishing performance with human participants.
neurips-2021-k-level-reasoning-for-zero-.tldr: Synchronously trained k-level reasoning enables competitive coordination with unfamiliar Hanabi partners, with further gains from co-training a best response.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to move a source probability distribution toward a fixed target using a relaxed version of KL divergence. This relaxation, KALE, comes from a regularized dual formulation restricted to a chosen function class. With a reproducing kernel Hilbert space as that class, KALE continuously interpolates between KL divergence and maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD.

KALE combines two properties relevant to distributions with different supports. Like MMD, it remains well defined even for mutually singular distributions. At the same time, it retains greater sensitivity than MMD to mismatches in where the distributions place their mass. The authors argue that this combination makes its gradient flow particularly suitable for targets concentrated on low-dimensional manifolds.

The paper proves global convergence of the flow under an assumption that its trajectories are sufficiently smooth. It also develops a particle implementation using initial samples from both source and target distributions. Experiments with that implementation support the stated properties of KALE. The contribution connects a distribution discrepancy, a conditional convergence result, and a sample-based procedure for realizing the flow.
neurips-2021-kale-flow-a-relaxed-kl-grad.tldr: KALE blends KL and MMD properties to define distribution flows across disjoint supports, with convergence under a smoothness assumption.

paragraphs: Using more clusters than the true number does not automatically make a clustering meaningless. The relevant question is whether the extra clusters mostly subdivide genuine groups or mix together points from different groups. This paper formalizes that question for generalized k-means by studying closeness to a refinement of the true cluster labels.

The authors provide conditions for both exact and approximate label recovery in this overfitted setting. Their guarantees apply to any constant-factor approximation to the k-means problem, so they do not depend on finding an exact optimum. The assumptions involve bounds on the maximum or average distance from data points to designated true centers.

The results are model-free: they do not require a particular probabilistic model for how the clusters were generated. Even the centers are flexible, provided the required distance bounds can be controlled. Applications to manifold clustering demonstrate the usefulness of this formulation. The main message is conditional but practical: overfitting the number of clusters can preserve meaningful label structure when the geometric conditions support a refinement.
neurips-2021-label-consistency-in-overfi.tldr: The paper gives geometric conditions under which overfitted generalized k-means preserves true groups through label refinements.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly assumes that the current state contains the information needed to describe what happens next. When an agent compresses rich observations into a learned representation, that Markov property can be lost. This paper asks how to learn an abstract state that retains the relevant decision-process structure.

The authors introduce conditions that are sufficient for a Markov abstract representation and prove the corresponding result. They then design a practical objective combining inverse-model estimation with temporal contrastive learning to approximately satisfy those conditions. The procedure works with online or offline training and does not require rewards, although it can use reward information when available.

Experiments on a visual gridworld and continuous-control benchmarks show representations that capture underlying domain structure. The authors report improved sample efficiency over state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning using visual features, often matching or exceeding performance with hand-designed compact states. The theoretical result establishes sufficient conditions, while the practical method targets them approximately. Together, these contributions connect a structural requirement for reinforcement learning to an empirically useful representation-learning objective.
neurips-2021-learning-markov-state-abstr.tldr: A representation-learning objective approximately enforces sufficient conditions for Markov state abstractions and improves reinforcement-learning sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Voting rules aggregate preferences in elections and in applications such as recommendation, search, and product design. Designing a suitable rule by hand is difficult when analytical tools do not cover every desired use case. This paper explores learning voting rules automatically using neural architectures designed to accept sets as inputs.

The authors study Set Transformers, fully connected graph networks, and DeepSets, providing theoretical and empirical support for their suitability. The networks can imitate established rules with compelling accuracy, including rules based on ranking positions and rules based on comparisons between alternatives. The examples cover Plurality and Borda as well as Kemeny, Copeland, and Maximin.

The models also learn near-optimal rules for different social welfare objectives, moving beyond imitation of existing procedures. The authors report that learned rules generalize well to voter utility distributions and election sizes absent from training. These findings support a flexible approach to preference aggregation: choose the welfare objective for a scenario and learn a rule suited to it, with empirical evidence of transfer across the tested election settings.
neurips-2021-learning-to-elect-6852c6340.tldr: Set-input neural networks can imitate established voting rules and learn near-optimal rules for different social welfare objectives.

paragraphs: Combining neural networks can improve prediction accuracy, confidence calibration, and robustness when evaluation data differ from training data. Conventional deep ensembles build this combination from separate random initializations of one fixed architecture. This paper investigates architectural variation as another source of useful diversity among ensemble members.

The authors propose two methods that automatically construct ensembles containing different architectures. Their selection implicitly balances each architecture’s individual predictive strength against what it contributes to the group’s diversity. This matters because the strongest collection need not consist of the individually strongest models: the ensemble also depends on how well its members complement one another.

Across several classification tasks and modern architecture search spaces, the resulting ensembles outperform deep ensembles in accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to dataset shift. Further analyses and ablations provide evidence that changing architectures increases diversity. Some resulting ensembles outperform deep ensembles even though their average individual member is weaker. The findings therefore support evaluating architectures as potential collaborators within an ensemble, alongside judging their standalone predictive performance.
neurips-2021-neural-ensemble-search-for-.tldr: Automatically combining different neural architectures improves ensemble accuracy, calibration, and robustness in the reported classification experiments.

paragraphs: Neural-network training objectives are highly nonconvex, yet gradient methods often work well in practice. Many theoretical explanations address particular architectures or learning setups using specialized arguments. This paper proposes a common optimization framework intended to organize those guarantees and make their shared structure easier to identify.

The framework introduces proxy convexity and proxy Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequalities. These conditions connect the original training objective to a proxy objective that gradient methods implicitly minimize. The useful guarantee is therefore expressed through that proxy, allowing the analysis to capture progress without requiring the original neural-network objective itself to be convex.

The authors prove efficient guarantees for stochastic gradient descent when an objective satisfies either proposed condition. They also show that many existing results for gradient-trained neural networks fit within this framework. The contribution is a unifying analytical language, together with optimization results for objectives meeting its requirements. Its scope remains conditional: the paper does not claim every neural network satisfies these properties, but shows that they account for a range of previously established guarantees.
neurips-2021-proxy-convexity-a-unified-f.tldr: Proxy convexity and proxy PL inequalities unify many gradient-based neural-network guarantees through implicitly minimized proxy objectives.

paragraphs: Video understanding depends on relationships across both space and time, especially the correspondences that convey motion. The paper argues that existing dynamic feature transforms, including self-attention, are limited in how they represent these relationships. This motivates a feature transformation built explicitly around the relational structure of video.

The proposed relational self-attention, or RSA, dynamically generates relational kernels and aggregates relational contexts. Both parts use spatiotemporal relationships to construct video representations. The approach extends the move from stationary convolution kernels to dynamic transforms by making relations themselves central to how features are generated and combined.

Experiments and ablation studies show substantial improvements over the convolutional and self-attention counterparts considered. The authors also report state-of-the-art action-recognition performance on motion-centric benchmarks, including Something-Something-V1 and V2, Diving48, and FineGym. These results support the usefulness of the relational design for tasks where motion is particularly important. The contribution is a concrete feature transform, backed by comparisons that connect its representation of video relationships to better recognition performance.
neurips-2021-relational-self-attention-w.tldr: Relational self-attention explicitly models spatiotemporal relationships and improves recognition on motion-centric video benchmarks.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial communication transmitting gradients. Sparsification reduces that traffic by sending only selected entries. The paper establishes that Top-k is communication-optimal under a fixed per-iteration entry budget, then asks whether allocating communication across the entire training run can produce better results.

The authors formulate a model that minimizes the sum of compression errors across iterations subject to a total communication budget. In this model, hard-threshold sparsification is optimal: a constant threshold determines how many entries are retained at each step. This permits the communication allocation to vary over training instead of fixing the same number of transmitted entries every iteration.

For hard-threshold sparsification with error feedback, the paper supplies convex and nonconvex convergence analyses. Within those analyses, it matches SGD’s asymptotic convergence and linear speedup, and avoids the data-heterogeneity impact associated with Top-k. Experiments across neural networks and logistic regression find greater communication efficiency than Top-k. The results show why optimizing compression over a whole training run can favor a different sparsification rule.
neurips-2021-rethinking-gradient-sparsif.tldr: Optimizing total compression error favors hard-threshold sparsification, which shows stronger communication efficiency than Top-k in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation and learning use data from a behavioral policy to reason about a different target policy. Importance sampling is a common tool for this purpose, but ordinary importance sampling can estimate poorly when the two policies are too dissimilar. This paper studies that failure and develops a transformed estimator.

The theoretical analysis introduces an anticoncentration bound that formalizes the undesirable behavior of the ordinary estimator. The proposed alternative uses transformations based on power means. Under certain conditions, the resulting estimator combines subgaussian concentration with differentiability in the target distribution. The first property controls estimation fluctuations, while the second keeps the estimator usable in procedures that optimize the target through derivatives.

The authors describe this combination as a first to their knowledge, with the stated conditions remaining essential to the claim. They also provide numerical simulations on synthetic examples and contextual bandits, comparing against off-policy evaluation and learning baselines. The central contribution is therefore a theoretical route to jointly obtaining concentration and differentiability, accompanied by empirical comparisons in settings relevant to policy evaluation and improvement.
neurips-2021-subgaussian-and-differentia.tldr: Power-mean transformations yield importance-sampling estimators that combine subgaussian concentration and target-distribution differentiability under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Sparse tensor PCA seeks a sparse unit vector hidden in a tensor corrupted by independent Gaussian noise. The model includes both sparse matrix PCA and tensor PCA, allowing the paper to examine how sparsity and tensor order jointly affect recovery. Its central question is how much computation is needed at different signal strengths.

For sparsity at most the square root of the ambient dimension, the authors give a family of algorithms ranging from polynomial-time methods toward exhaustive search. A tuning parameter trades longer runtime for recovery at weaker signal-to-noise ratios. The guarantees recover leading matrix-case results and extend to multiple sparse signals when their supports are disjoint, without dependence on the number of signals in the recovery threshold.

The paper complements these algorithms with low-degree likelihood-ratio analysis, providing rigorous evidence for signal-strength versus runtime tradeoffs. This is evidence through a particular analytical framework, rather than an unrestricted computational impossibility claim. Together, the results connect known sparse PCA and tensor PCA behavior and reveal a more intricate interaction among dimension, sparsity, and tensor order.
neurips-2021-the-complexity-of-sparse-te.tldr: A family of sparse tensor PCA algorithms trades computation for weaker signal requirements, supported by low-degree evidence about computational limits.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from previous tasks to help train models for new ones. A common protocol trains each task-specific solver on a support set and evaluates it on a separate query set. This paper explores evaluating the solver against a target model that is optimal or sufficiently good for that task.

Target models can supply more informative supervision, but constructing them is computationally expensive. The authors investigate using them for only a small fraction of tasks. In their few-shot learning application, they create target models by fine-tuning a pretrained network on hard tasks, then use knowledge distillation to align task-specific solvers with those targets.

The empirical findings show that this limited use of target models can substantially improve classic meta-learning algorithms without consuming many resources. This makes the support/target protocol a practical supplement to the more familiar support/query setup. The contribution is a way to obtain useful model-based supervision selectively, concentrating target-model construction on part of the task collection while allowing the resulting guidance to improve the broader meta-learning process.
neurips-2021-towards-enabling-meta-learn.tldr: Providing target models for a small fraction of tasks improves few-shot meta-learning through selective knowledge distillation.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning agent may solve its training environment yet fail in other environments that appear similar. This paper studies how many queries are required to learn agents that generalize across environments. It asks whether shared structure is enough to make that learning problem computationally manageable in terms of query complexity.

The authors define Weak Proximity: environments have highly similar transition and reward functions and share a policy attaining optimal value. They prove that even this structure does not ensure efficient generalization in the worst case. The difficulty remains when each environment individually admits efficient recovery of an optimal linear policy and the learner has access to a generative model.

The lower bound also applies to learning representations for efficient generalization across environments. On the positive side, the paper introduces Strong Proximity and proves that it is sufficient for efficient generalization. The contrast identifies a gap between intuitive similarity and a stronger condition that supports a tractability guarantee. Strong Proximity is established as sufficient, without the abstract claiming that it is necessary.
neurips-2021-when-is-generalizable-reinf.tldr: Similar environments sharing an optimal policy can still make generalization intractable, while a stronger proximity condition suffices for efficiency.
